Rules: - Do not infer the person's thoughts, feelings, intelligence, diagnosis, or preferences. - Do not narrow or replace their existing communication system. - Treat speech, vocalizations, gestures, gaze, body movement, signs, real objects, photographs, visual scenes, symbols, AAC, typing, texting, drawing, writing, switch access, and scanning as possible communication routes when I say they are relevant. - Speak directly to the person in the finished material. - Include how to say or confirm YES and NO when I provide that information. - Make room for NO, STOP, BREAK, FINISHED, HELP, NOT SURE, and SOMETHING ELSE when appropriate. - Separate confirmed facts from a support person's interpretation. - If information is missing, leave a blank rather than inventing it. - Keep private medical, school, and family history out unless I explicitly say it is necessary. - Use short sentences, generous spacing, and concrete wording. - Output two versions: (1) a one-page printable field card and (2) a plain-text version that can be pasted into an email, note, or care handoff. MaternalPick one ritual that is not logistics: a ten-minute coffee-and-music reset, a walk, a favorite shop, a manicure at home, reading side by side, one easy meal made together. SiblingCreate one thing that belongs to the siblings: a playlist, a snack run, a pool ritual, a recurring show, a private joke, a short errand. Participation should stay voluntary. GrandparentChoose repeatable over impressive: the same diner booth, same short walk, same photo album, same store, same simple Saturday snack. Predictability can become tradition. Co-parent / partnerTrade one whole responsibility rather than “helping” with pieces of it: Saturday breakfast, the pool bag, school paperwork, the pharmacy run, bedtime setup, or outing prep. Caregiver / support personHave a relationship lane that is yours: swimming, walks, music, cooking, basketball, library time. Support the person’s own choices inside it. Whole familyKeep one plan short enough that everyone can imagine doing it again. A family identity can be built from tiny rituals repeated over time.
